result.content_text:
# The Witness

The body was three days old when Mira found it.

She almost missed it. The collapsed section of Sublevel 9 had been cordoned off for two years, ever since the pressure seals failed and the tunnel flooded. Nobody came down here. The maintenance logs showed zero entries since the accident. That was why she'd chosen this route, she needed somewhere the cameras didn't reach.

She pulled the body from behind a rusted conduit pipe. Male, mid-forties, wearing a Meridian Corporation jumpsuit with the sleeve insignia of a senior engineer. His face was intact. That surprised her. Three days in Sublevel 9 should have left more damage.

Mira crouched and held her wristlight closer. No visible wounds. No bruising on the throat. She checked his hands, clean, no defensive marks. She photographed everything with her personal lens, not the department-issued one.

The difference mattered., -

She'd been a Compliance Investigator for Meridian Station for eleven years. The station was a cylinder fourteen kilometers long, orbiting a brown dwarf at the edge of the Kepler Belt. Forty thousand people lived here. Most of them worked extraction or processing. A few hundred worked administration. And a handful, like Mira, worked enforcement.

The dead man's name was Tobias Venn. She confirmed it when she got back to her office and ran his face through personnel records. Senior Engineer, Atmospheric Systems. Employed by Meridian for nine years. Clean record. No disciplinary flags.

His last logged location was the Level 3 cafeteria, three days ago at 0800 hours.

Between 0800 and whenever he ended up behind a conduit pipe in a flooded sublevel, there was nothing. No card swipes. No camera appearances. No comm activity.

Mira sat with that for a long moment.

Then she filed a missing person report instead of a death report, listed her discovery site as Sublevel 7, and went home to eat dinner., -

Her apartment was small. Most apartments on the station were. She had a window, which was a luxury, a thick port looking out at the brown dwarf's dim, rust-colored glow. She ate rice and reconstituted protein and watched the dwarf's cloud bands shift.

She thought about Tobias Venn.

Atmospheric Systems engineers had access to the station's environmental controls. Air recycling, pressure management, temperature regulation. The kind of access that, in the wrong hands, could do serious damage to forty thousand people.

She thought about why someone might want him dead.

She thought about why someone had been careful enough to leave no marks.

Then she thought about the other thing, the thing she'd noticed but hadn't photographed, hadn't written down, hadn't even fully acknowledged to herself yet.

The access panel behind the conduit pipe. The one Venn's body had been blocking.

It had been recently opened. The seal residue was fresh, maybe a week old. Someone had been in there, and then someone had put a body in front of it., -

In the morning she went to see Director Callum Osei.

Osei ran Compliance for the entire station. He was a compact man with careful eyes and a habit of keeping his desk completely clear of anything. No papers, no terminals, no coffee cups. Just a flat surface between him and whoever he was talking to.

"Tobias Venn," Mira said. She placed a single printed photograph on the desk. Personnel file image, not her lens capture. "He's been missing for three days. I'd like to open a formal investigation."

Osei looked at the photo. "Missing persons is handled by Security."

"Security hasn't flagged it. I'm flagging it now."

"Why?"

"Because he worked Atmospheric Systems and he's been gone three days with no trace. That's unusual for someone with his access level."

Osei picked up the photograph and looked at it for a moment, then set it back down. "I'll pass it to Security. They'll handle the standard protocol."

"I'd like to run a parallel inquiry. Given his systems access."

"That's not standard procedure."

"No," Mira agreed.

Osei looked at her. She looked back. After a moment he said, "I'll consider it."

She took the photograph and left., -

She went to Atmospheric Systems next. The department occupied a wide section of Level 4, all exposed ductwork and monitoring panels and the constant low hum of the recyclers. The smell was different here, cleaner, somehow, with an undertone of ozone.

The shift supervisor was a woman named Dani Roark. Late thirties, tired eyes, the kind of competent that came from doing a hard job for a long time.

"Tobias?" Dani said. "He called in sick three days ago. I assumed it was the stomach thing going around."

"Did he seem unusual before that? Stressed, distracted?"

Dani thought about it. "He was working late a lot. Last couple weeks. I figured it was the pressure calibration project, we've had some anomalies in the secondary loop."

"What kind of anomalies?"

"Readings that don't match. The sensors say one thing, the manual checks say another." Dani paused. "Tobias was the one who flagged it, actually. He was pretty concerned."

"Who did he report it to?"

"Me. I passed it up to Engineering Management." Another pause. "That was about ten days ago. I haven't heard anything back."

Mira wrote nothing down. She thanked Dani and left., -

She spent the afternoon in the records archive, which was a room that smelled of recycled air and old plastic and was staffed by a single automated terminal. She pulled ten years of atmospheric maintenance logs and read through them in a corner where the ceiling camera had a blind spot she'd identified three years ago during a different investigation.

The secondary pressure loop anomalies were there. Tobias had logged them carefully, with timestamps and sensor readings and manual verification data. The discrepancies were small, fractions of a percent, but they were consistent, and they'd been getting larger over time.

She cross-referenced the affected sections. They all corresponded to a single residential block on Level 6. About two thousand people lived there.

She sat with that.

Then she went deeper into the logs and found something else. Maintenance records for the access panels in Sublevel 9. Specifically, the panel behind the conduit pipe where she'd found Tobias Venn's body.

The panel connected to the secondary pressure loop.

Someone had accessed it eight days ago. The record showed an authorized entry under the credentials of a Level 3 maintenance technician named Piotr Salas.

Mira looked up Piotr Salas.

He'd been transferred to Meridian Station's sister facility six months ago. He was currently 800 million kilometers away., -

She ate dinner at the Level 2 commissary instead of going home. She needed to think in a place with people around her.

The commissary was loud with the end-of-shift crowd. Workers in extraction suits, still carrying the faint chemical smell of the processing bays. Families. A group of teenagers arguing about something on a shared screen. The ordinary texture of a place where forty thousand people lived their lives.

She ordered coffee and thought about what she knew.

Someone had accessed a panel in the secondary pressure loop using stolen credentials. Tobias Venn had been investigating anomalies in that same loop. Tobias Venn was now dead, hidden in a location that was supposed to be inaccessible, with no marks on his body.

The panel connected to the pressure systems serving two thousand people on Level 6.

The anomalies had been getting worse.

She thought about what she didn't know. What the panel had been used for. Whether the anomalies were the cause of something or the symptom of something. Whether Tobias had found an answer before he died.

She thought about who had access to stolen credentials, who knew the flooded sublevel well enough to use it as a disposal site, and who had enough authority to keep Engineering Management from responding to a flagged safety concern for ten days.

She drank her coffee and watched the families eat dinner., -

There was a man named Harlan Brice who worked in Station Infrastructure Management. He was three levels above Engineering Management in the org chart. He had been on the station for fourteen years, which was three years longer than Mira. He had a reputation for getting things done and for being the kind of person who understood how the station really worked, as opposed to how it was supposed to work.

Mira had crossed paths with him twice in eleven years. Both times she'd come away with the feeling that he was watching her more carefully than the situation required.

She went to find him.

His office was on Level 2, near the administrative core. A real office, not a cubicle, a door that closed, a window, a desk with actual objects on it. He was there when she arrived, reading something on a tablet. He looked up without surprise.

"Investigator Mira Chen," he said. "Sit down."

She sat.

"You've been busy," he said.

"I have some questions about the secondary pressure loop anomalies in Section 6."

"That's an Engineering Management matter."

"They haven't responded to the flag."

"These things take time."

"Tobias Venn flagged it ten days ago."

Brice set down his tablet. He had a still quality to him, like someone who had learned a long time ago that most of the information in a conversation came from watching the other person. "Tobias Venn is on medical leave."

"He's been missing for three days."

"Medical leave," Brice said again.

Mira looked at him. "The access panel in Sublevel 9, Section 12-C. It was accessed eight days ago using the credentials of a technician who's been off-station for six months."

Something moved behind Brice's eyes. Very small, very fast.

"That's a Security matter," he said.

"I'd like to know what's behind that panel."

"I don't know what you're referring to."

"The panel connects to the secondary pressure loop for Level 6. If someone has been tampering with it, two thousand people are at risk."

Brice stood up. He was taller than she'd remembered. "I think you should talk to Director Osei about the scope of your current investigation."

"I have," Mira said. "He's considering it."

"Then you should wait for his decision."

She stood as well. "Of course," she said. "Thank you for your time."

She walked out., -

In the corridor outside Brice's office, she stopped and stood still for a moment with her back against the wall.

She had made a mistake. She'd shown him what she knew before she had anything solid enough to use. She'd wanted to see his reaction, and she'd gotten it, but now he knew she was looking.

She had maybe a few hours before something happened. Either the evidence disappeared, or she did.

She went to find Dani Roark., -

"I need you to do a manual inspection of the secondary loop," Mira said. "Right now. Not a sensor check, physical eyes on the hardware, from the access panel in Sublevel 9 all the way through."

Dani stared at her. "Sublevel 9 is flooded."

"Section 12 isn't. The flood is further east."

"I'd need authorization from, "

"I'm authorizing it. Compliance investigation. I'm logging it right now." Mira was already typing on her wristpad. "I need you to go now, and I need you to take photographs of everything you see, on a personal device, not department-issued equipment."

Dani looked at her for a long moment. "Is this about Tobias?"

"Yes."

Dani pulled off her department ID badge and put it in her pocket. Then she picked up a personal comm unit from her desk drawer. "Okay," she said., -

Mira spent the next hour in the archive room, working fast. She copied everything she'd found, the maintenance logs, the anomaly reports, Tobias's flagged records, the access log for the panel under Piotr Salas's stolen credentials, and packaged it into an encrypted file. She sent it to three places: her personal off-station storage account, the Kepler Belt Regional Authority's public evidence submission portal, and a journalist she'd met once at a conference who worked for an independent news service.

Then she went back to Sublevel 9., -

The body was still there. She hadn't expected it to be. She photographed it again, properly this time, with timestamps and location markers, and uploaded everything to the same three places.

She was crouching over Tobias Venn's body when she heard footsteps in the tunnel behind her.

She stood and turned.

Two men she didn't recognize. Station Security uniforms, but she knew most of Security and she didn't know these faces. They were carrying restraint equipment.

"Investigator Chen," the taller one said. "Director Osei has asked us to escort you to his office."

"Of course," she said. "Let me just finish documenting this scene."

"Now, please."

She looked at Tobias Venn. His face was still intact. He'd found something, and he'd been careful, and it hadn't been enough.

She put her lens away and walked toward the two men., -

They took her to a room that wasn't Osei's office. It was a holding room in the Security section, small and white and without windows. She sat at the table and waited.

Harlan Brice came in after twenty minutes.

He sat across from her. He had the same still quality, but something underneath it was different now. Tighter.

"What did you send?" he said.

"I don't know what you mean."

"The encrypted transfer from the archive terminal. We flagged it in real-time. What was in it?"

"Compliance investigation files. Standard procedure for off-site backup."

"The Regional Authority submission portal isn't standard backup."

She said nothing.

Brice leaned forward slightly. "This station runs on certain arrangements. You've been here eleven years. You understand how things work."

"I understand that two thousand people on Level 6 might be breathing compromised air."

"That's being handled."

"By who? The same people who didn't respond to Tobias Venn's flag for ten days?"

"Venn was a complication."

The word landed in the room and sat there.

"He found the modifications," Mira said. "In the pressure loop. What were they for?"

Brice was quiet for a moment. Then: "There are contracts. Long-term infrastructure contracts with certain parties who require certain guarantees about the station's operational parameters."

"What kind of guarantees?"

"The kind that require the residential population in Section 6 to be relocated within the next eighteen months. The modifications to the pressure loop were designed to make that section gradually uninhabitable. Slowly enough that it would look like equipment degradation."

Mira stared at him.

"Two thousand people," she said.

"Who would be relocated. With compensation. To better facilities."

"Relocated where? Why?"

"Section 6 sits above a thermal vent cluster that wasn't in the original survey data. The extraction value is significant."

She thought about the families in the commissary. The teenagers arguing over a screen. The workers coming off shift.

"Tobias figured it out," she said.

"He was going to go to the Regional Authority directly. We couldn't allow that."

"How did you kill him? There were no marks."

"Atmospheric Systems engineers have access to a great many things," Brice said. He said it without any particular emotion, the way you'd explain a mechanical process.

Mira nodded slowly. "And now?"

"Now you've created a problem. The file you sent, we can have it flagged as fraudulent. Your credentials, your access history, can be reframed. A Compliance Investigator who went rogue. Fabricated evidence. It happens."

"I sent it to a journalist."

"Journalists receive fraudulent tips constantly."

"She's good at her job."

Brice studied her. "So are we.", -

She sat in the holding room for six hours. Nobody came. They brought her water once.

She had time to think about whether she'd done enough. Whether the files were complete enough, clear enough, whether the journalist would know what she was looking at. Whether the Regional Authority's submission portal had actually received the package or whether it had been intercepted.

She thought about Tobias Venn, who had done everything right and still ended up behind a conduit pipe in a flooded sublevel.

She thought about what the difference was between them.

The difference was that she'd sent the files before walking into Brice's office. Tobias, probably, had tried to handle it through proper channels first.

She hoped that was enough of a difference., -

The door opened at hour seven. It was a woman she didn't recognize, wearing a Regional Authority jacket.

"Investigator Chen?" she said. "I'm Deputy Marshal Sera Yun. We received your submission about four hours ago. We've been verifying." She paused. "We've also been in contact with the journalist. She's already filed."

Mira stood up slowly. Her back ached from the chair.

"Harlan Brice," she said.

"In custody. Along with Director Osei and two others." Yun paused again. "We found the body. Tobias Venn."

"I know."

"His family has been notified."

Mira walked to the door. In the corridor outside, she could hear the station's normal sounds, the hum of the recyclers, the distant clang of the processing bays, the ordinary noise of forty thousand people going about their lives.

"The pressure loop," she said.

"Engineering teams are already in Section 12. We'll have a full assessment within the day. The residents of Level 6 are being notified as a precaution." Yun looked at her. "You did good work."

Mira thought about Tobias Venn doing good work. She thought about where that had gotten him.

"He did the work," she said. "I just made sure it survived."

She walked out into the corridor and stood for a moment with the station's hum around her, the recycled air moving through the vents, the rust-colored light of the brown dwarf coming through a porthole at the far end of the hall.

Then she went to find somewhere to sit down and write her report.
